summary:
Sarawak stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, and acts of gross indecency are separately punishable on the same scale. The provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Sarawak is one of the 13 states whose Sharia enactments criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor is not exposed to that layer; enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a trans visitor's documents will carry their original markers at immigration and in any identity check.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. A study accompanying an August 2022 report interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 and documented conversion practices, discrimination and violence against them.

Enforcement recorded since the 2018 election includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in which at least 20 LGBT people were arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue that netted twenty men, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 plans in Johor to open conversion-therapy centres. None of these incidents took place in Sarawak, but each arose under the statutes that govern Sarawak, and the raid-based pattern is the exposure a visitor would encounter.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees as of June 2021. The federal provisions apply in Sarawak in full.
tangentialFactors:
The country profile underlying these findings was last updated on 16 December 2025, so the enforcement picture it records is current rather than historical.

Conversion practice is a distinct axis of exposure alongside criminalisation: the August 2022 report by Human Rights Watch with Justice for Sisters is devoted to anti-LGBT conversion practices, discrimination and violence, and Johor's November 2023 announcement of conversion-therapy centres indicates official sponsorship of that approach in at least one state.

Sarawak's position within the 13 states with cross-dressing enactments is typical rather than exceptional; the specific incidents cited here occurred in Kuala Lumpur, Terengganu and Johor, and no Sarawak-specific raid or prosecution appears in the current inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents of Sarawak who are Muslim fall under the state Sharia enactment on cross-dressing, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, with investigation and arrest carried out by the state Islamic religious department rather than the police.

Sarawak residents of any faith remain subject to sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code and to the gross-indecency provisions, which carry up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes are a resident-facing institution: at least 1,733 people had attended them by June 2021.

Because no legal gender-recognition procedure exists, residents have no route to amend the gender marker on national identity documents, and reported discrimination and violence against transgender people are documented as routine.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Sarawak-specific enforcement incident, arrest or prosecution appears in the source inventory supplied for this pass; the enforcement examples available are from Kuala Lumpur, Terengganu and Johor, so the Sarawak pattern of enforcement is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Whether Sarawak's Sharia enactment also bars women from posing as men is not sourced; three of the 13 states are recorded as doing so, without naming them.

Whether conversion-therapy or "rehabilitation" provision exists within Sarawak itself is not sourced; the documented centres are a Johor plan and the attendance figures are national.

The inventory does not itemise the maximum penalty for gross indecency separately from the 20-year maximum recorded for carnal intercourse against the order of nature, so the two are reported here on the same scale as the source gives them.
